formNote: The modern split is visual, not etymological. The early graph sets a sun above a second element whose meaning is debated (a grain field, measuring under the sun, the sun in the east). The Shuowen: abbreviated 重 “weight” with 曏 as phonetic.
summary: A word that keeps an Old Chinese derivation visible: level-tone liáng is the act of measuring or weighing; departing-tone liàng is the result — capacity, magnanimity, and in Buddhist logic, pramāṇa, the measure of valid knowing.
placement: Low on the left wing, close to 無 — the two halves of 無量, “immeasurable”.

readings.extraNote: Readings beyond Unihan’s list, added by Baracus from general knowledge; not yet checked.

satellites.title: Measuring and Measure
satellites.evidence: liáng (< *[r]aŋ): to measure, weigh, deliberate (測量, 思量). liàng (< *[r]aŋ-s): the result — quantity, capacity, magnanimity (器量), and the immeasurable (無量). The same *-s derivation seen in 為 wéi / wèi.

satellites.title: Valid Means of Knowing
satellites.evidence: In Buddhist epistemology, 量 renders pramāṇa, a valid means of knowing. The Nyāyapraveśa distinguishes 現量, direct perception free from conceptual discrimination, from 比量, inference through evidential signs. They are two ways of knowing, not two degrees of certainty.

checked.note: The passage distinguishes 現量 from 比量 and describes inference through signs. Sanskrit equivalences are not verified by this Chinese passage alone.

satellites.caveat: Xuanzang translated this primer by Śaṅkarasvāmin. It is not Dignāga’s Pramāṇasamuccaya; the Chinese translation of the latter is attributed to Yijing and is lost.

satellites.title: The Immeasurables
satellites.evidence: With 無, 量 forms 無量 (apramāṇa, amita): boundless, beyond measure — the Four Immeasurable Minds 慈悲喜捨, and Amitābha and Amitāyus, Buddha of Immeasurable Light (無量光) and Immeasurable Life (無量壽).

satellites.title: Measure and Moderation
satellites.evidence: Malay ukuran and sukatan, like French mesure, span quantitative measurement and a sense of proportion — “à sa mesure”, within one’s measure — much as liàng spans quantity and capacity of character.
